HomeNotes: 12/6/2023 Foster Notes 11/30/23 - 12/6/23: She is super easy button so would be an easy foster for anybody who will give her a chance! She is the perfect dog to get through HW treatment. She is so appreciative of affection and will try to army crawl her way to be as close to you as possible on the couch. She snarled at my dog on a walk when he got a little energetic near her but otherwise she is amazing on walks and non reactive to anything else, she briefly tried to chase one squirrel. We never fully integrated her and our dog, she has been more alert around him in the house so we mostly kept them separated. I think she would prefer to be the only pet in the home! No signs of stranger danger and she hasn’t barked at all, she’s very quiet and just whimpers for a few seconds when she’s left alone. I think she has been abused in the past, she cowers like she thinks you’re going to hit her and she is extremely responsive to “no”. She’s very eager to please. Not one accident in the house after 2 years in the shelter! I love her so much, the best girl. She is SO loving and extremely cuddly. She does come at you and is a little jumpy with big energy when she hasn’t seen you for a minute but it’s very brief and she settles quickly.

10/25/2023 A random car stopped with a random big dog hanging out the window barking, this person then got out of her car and approached the fosters yard with Marty on leash and her other two dogs in yard they all got really amped up and over stimulated  by the stranger and strange dog approaching to the point where the resident dog turned and redirected on Marty. Marty and the resident dog then latched on to one another, Marty was the only dog on leash, the foster struggled to keep them apart, but they kept latching, the neighbor came to help and was bit by Marty in the process of breaking up the dog fight. 

10/26/2023 10/25/23 I took Marty and my two dogs out to the yard. We have been keeping my one dog that he previously got into a fight with a Marty separate, but they have been doing better. So I took them outside and kept Marty on a leash in the yard to help him stay calm and work on boundaries. Everything was going well. Then someone I do not know parked in front of the fence and a large lab put its head out of the window and started barking in a bit of an aggressive way. My dogs reacted and ran up to the fence and started barking back. The owner then got out of the car and put the dog on a leash and brought it up to the fence. The lab dog was barking aggressively at my dogs, and they were getting very agitated. I kept Marty at a distance since he was on the leash. I called out to her and asked her to move away from the fence. She didn't really respond, and she looked like she was going to open the gate to come in. I then became scared she was going to enter, and I don't think she lives here so maybe she did not know the rules. I moved closer to try to get my dogs away from the fence. In his agitation my dog turned around and went for Marty and that is when they started fighting. I tried to get them apart, but they had latched onto each other's faces and wouldn't let go. A neighbor saw what was happening and he came into the yard and was trying to help me separate them. He managed to reach in and pull Marty's head back, but my dog was still trying to get to him. I think Marty was scared and in all the chaos he bit my neighbor's arm. I don't believe Marty intentionally bit my neighbor but was just in fight or flight mode. My neighbor went to the hospital, and I did get in contact, and they said the hospital notified animal control. I provided the vaccine records for both dogs. I asked for pictures of the injury, but they have not provided them so far. I was a bit alarmed to find out that Marty's rabies shots were not up to date. I am afraid that could put me in a very bad situation where I could face legal issues. I had just assumed all fosters would be up to date on vaccines. I know my neighbors were understandably upset and I offered to pay any medical expenses. I feel so horrible because I don't feel like it was completely Marty's fault so it will be devastating if his options are limited because of this. I don't think he is at risk of biting any people, but I do think he would be better off in a foster and home without other dogs or animals. I think with an experienced owner and training he would do very well, and he was already making great progress. So this is really heartbreaking, and I really am blaming myself. I think there is always a risk when you reach into a dog fight of getting bitten and I think that is what happened here.

10/25/2023 A random car stopped with a random big dog hanging out the window barking, this person then got out of her car and approached the fosters yard with Marty on leash and her other two dogs in yard they all got really amped up and over stimulated  by the stranger and strange dog approaching to the point where the resident dog turned and redirected on Marty. 10/26/2023 10/25/23 I took Marty and my two dogs out to the yard. We have been keeping my one dog that he previously got into a fight with a Marty separate, but they have been doing better. So I took them outside and kept Marty on a leash in the yard to help him stay calm and work on boundaries. Everything was going well. Then someone I do not know parked in front of the fence and a large lab put its head out of the window and started barking in a bit of an aggressive way. My dogs reacted and ran up to the fence and started barking back. The owner then got out of the car and put the dog on a leash and brought it up to the fence. The lab dog was barking aggressively at my dogs, and they were getting very agitated. I kept Marty at a distance since he was on the leash. I called out to her and asked her to move away from the fence. She didn't really respond, and she looked like she was going to open the gate to come in. I then became scared she was going to enter, and I don't think she lives here so maybe she did not know the rules. I moved closer to try to get my dogs away from the fence. In his agitation my dog turned around and went for Marty and that is when they started fighting. I tried to get them apart, but they had latched onto each other's faces and wouldn't let go. A neighbor saw what was happening and he came into the yard and was trying to help me separate them. He managed to reach in and pull Marty's head back, but my dog was still trying to get to him. I think Marty was scared and in all the chaos he bit my neighbor's arm. I don't believe Marty intentionally bit my neighbor but was just in fight or flight mode. My neighbor went to the hospital, and I did get in contact, and they said the hospital notified animal control. I provided the vaccine records for both dogs. I asked for pictures of the injury, but they have not provided them so far. I was a bit alarmed to find out that Marty's rabies shots were not up to date. I am afraid that could put me in a very bad situation where I could face legal issues. I had just assumed all fosters would be up to date on vaccines. I know my neighbors were understandably upset and I offered to pay any medical expenses. I feel so horrible because I don't feel like it was completely Marty's fault so it will be devastating if his options are limited because of this. I don't think he is at risk of biting any people, but I do think he would be better off in a foster and home without other dogs or animals. I think with an experienced owner and training he would do very well, and he was already making great progress. So this is really heartbreaking, and I really am blaming myself. I think there is always a risk when you reach into a dog fight of getting bitten and I think that is what happened here.

4/4/2024 Spanky Training/Handling Tips:? Drop off enrichment to help him expend some mental energy if possible before taking him out. (Frozen enrichment can be found in the white freezer located in the back sally port)? Before opening the kennel, show him your treats and ask him to “sit” and then give him a treat when he sits. If he’s excited, it  may take a few asks before he responds. Then use the treat on the other side of the loop trick to get the leash on him.? Keep treats visible as you walk and throw them on the ground for him to “find it” until you get outside or he shifts his attention to his surroundings ? If he bites at the leash, continue walking while ignoring the behavior. If you are in a contained area, intersperse dropping the leash in response to any increase in tugging. As soon as there is a slight pause or decrease in intensity, redirect him with “down” and/or “sit” and then give him a treat with verbal praise. Repeat as needed.? Start walking again, a treat + praise or throwing treat for him to "find it" every few steps ? If he starts to bite again, correct him by saying “eh” and then reset his behavior with “down” or “sit” followed by treat + praise. Then resume walking ? Once biting stops, keep him engaged and reinforce good walking with intermittent treats thrown for him to find? When un/re-leashing, first ask him to “sit” first and then give him a treat.  ** If you try to pull the leash away from him, he will tug back. If you ignore, drop the leash (he's not a runner), and redirect him with a command, then he will drop the leash to fetch the treat! ** Continue asking him to "find it" until he is leading the walk and no longer looking at you. At this point, he'll be easy on leash ** Any time you need to adjust/tighten/handle the leash, ask him to do something and reward him right as you do it (this results in him focusing on what you want him to do vs. the leash you're adjusting)

4/4/2024 Spanky Training/Handling Tips:? Drop off enrichment to help him expend some mental energy if possible before taking him out. (Frozen enrichment can be found in the white freezer located in the back sally port)? Before opening the kennel, show him your treats and ask him to “sit” and then give him a treat when he sits. If he’s excited, it  may take a few asks before he responds. Then use the treat on the other side of the loop trick to get the leash on him.? Keep treats visible as you walk and throw them on the ground for him to “find it” until you get outside or he shifts his attention to his surroundings ? If he bites at the leash, continue walking while ignoring the behavior. If you are in a contained area, intersperse dropping the leash in response to any increase in tugging. As soon as there is a slight pause or decrease in intensity, redirect him with “down” and/or “sit” and then give him a treat with verbal praise. Repeat as needed.? Start walking again, a treat + praise or throwing treat for him to "find it" every few steps ? If he starts to bite again, correct him by saying “eh” and then reset his behavior with “down” or “sit” followed by treat + praise. Then resume walking ? Once biting stops, keep him engaged and reinforce good walking with intermittent treats thrown for him to find? When un/re-leashing, first ask him to “sit” first and then give him a treat.  ** If you try to pull the leash away from him, he will tug back. If you ignore, drop the leash (he's not a runner), and redirect him with a command, then he will drop the leash to fetch the treat! ** Continue asking him to "find it" until he is leading the walk and no longer looking at you. At this point, he'll be easy on leash ** Any time you need to adjust/tighten/handle the leash, ask him to do something and reward him right as you do it (this results in him focusing on what you want him to do vs. the leash you're adjusting)

DogTest: 6/29/2024 Chocolate Chip was put in the 500s and was shaking, so Jan pulled her out to the multipurpose room. We brought Katara in to see if she would be more comfortable with a confident dog in the room. Both dogs were on leash. When Katara came into the room, Chocolate Chip immediately had a low tail and barked at Katara with tense body language. Katara looked over at her and walked away. Jan and I continued walking them around the room in big circles (always at least 10 feet away). Chocolate Chip would stop walking and stare at Katara, then go back to sniffing and looking out the window. Timya walked into the room and gave each dog treats and then left the room. We continued walking for a bit. Whenever Chocolate Chip and Katara got within 10 feet of each other, Chocolate Chip started barking and snarling at Katara. Katara reacted by doing the same. We ended the dog test.
Behavior:
4/25/2024 Scared but easily handled. showed signs of fear, startles easily, tense muscles, frozen, trying to hide, not taking treats..

5/2/2024 We visited Chocolate Chip inside her kennel.  She backed into the wall inside her kennel.  Tossed treats she accepted them from a distance as we sat on her bed and the floor.  She did come up and sniff me briefly and then added space between us.  So timid, would benefit from a volunteer advocate.

6/12/2024 incessant barking, reacting at other dogs and stimuli by her kennel. if you approach her kennel, she cowers away. I think she may need to move to a quieter section. 

6/29/2024 I was moving Chocolate Chip from the flex to an indoor/outdoor and she was evasive of the leash at first. Gingerly walked out of the kennel then loosened up on the way to 500. Once the dogs started barking at her she pancaked and refused to go inside the new run. I was able to coax her in but she layed flat in the back of the kennel and would not move or pick her head up.
Cat Interaction: Could do well with proper introductions
Potty Skills: Has done well in a home.
Cuddle Meter: Let's get to know each other before cuddling

Yes, April 27,2025 until May 1, 2025General Personality Charley is a loving dog who is very energetic and loves to play. She is friendly with other dogs is and always want to play with them. She is a little shy when it comes to people unless she smells other dogs on them. She gives lots of kiss and wants to snuggle when she is ready to go to sleep. Charley is an active dog and would like to eat and play all day if she could. She is an absolute great dog for a family with an who enjoys being outdoors. She loves to go for rides in the car.Daily Routine Mon - Fridays she wakes up between 500am and 650am. I take her out for her first bathroom break within 10 minutes of waking up. We snuggle or play for about 30 mins then she eats breakfast. She eats breakfast between 730 and 830am. She lays down or sleep until 1015am. I take her out for her second bathroom break between 11am and 12 am. We will play for 15 minutes. She eats lunch at 3pm. She will lay down for a nap and wakes up around 4/430pm. I typically take her out for her final bathroom break between 530 and 630pm but it can later. She usually goes to sleep at 7pm. Saturday varies based on what I have planned for the day. Sundays vary based on what I have planned after worship service, but typically she is up by 7am. She goes out and eat shortly after. She is in the crate from 8am to 1230pm. When I return home she goes out for a bathroom break and then we play or relax. She eats lunch at 3pm and her last bathroom break is at 6pm. We may go for a walk afterwards. She goes to sleep around 7pm.What food do they eat? Ollie's human grade dog good: moist (pork and vegs) and dry.What would be an ideal home and family for your foster? A young family with children over the age of 6 and preferably one other pet. Or a mobile older adult that does does have any physical restrictions. They should live in a house (with minimal stairs) with big backyard for her to run around and play in.On a scale of 1 to 5 how housetrained are they? 4Does your foster use a kennel without excessive barking/whining, escape attempts, or destruction? Charley does not whine, bark, escape, or tries to destroy her kennel. Majority of the time she goes in with no problems.Where do they sleep at night? In her bed on my bedroom floorDo they sleep through the night? Depends the her last bathroom break.Has he / she been exposed to any kids? If yes, what ages? How did it go? I am not around young children on a regular basis. The youngest person she interacts with is eleven years old and they are best friends.Has he / she been exposed to any cats? If yes, how did it go? She has not been directly exposed to cats but she sees stray cats in the neighborhood. I do not allow her to interact with them.Do they prefer men or women? WomenDoes he / she live with another dog? No, she does not live with any other dogs.Has he / she been around other dogs? Yes, Charley interacts with other dogs. She is very playful with other dogs unless they do not show interest in her. I gave not seen her afraid of other dogs.Does he / she know any basic commands? Which ones (Sit, stay, come, lay down, etc) ? Yes, Charley knows the basic commands of sit, stay, wait, eat, and come.Is your foster dog leash reactive? What makes them bark/lunge on leash? No, Charley is not leash reactive. She rarely barks and never lunges.What devices do you use to walk your dog? (Type of harness, collar, etc) I use a collar to walk her.Leash Walking Rating 4How does your foster do in the car? Charley gets excited when she gets in the car to the point she has to use the bathroom shortly after she gets in. She likes to be next to the driver and must be able to see out the front windshield. She prefers to listen to jazz while resting her head on the driver's shoulder.How does your foster do for a bath? I take her to the groomer and they say she does well.Energy level 4How much exercise does it take to tire them out? 10 to 15 minsIf they don't get enough exercise, what happens? She will do zoomies for a few minutes, jump around and on you, or find a toy to play with.A perfect day for your foster would include ____________? A day off from work and other obligations to take Charley to a trail for a couple of hours and walk around until she gets tired. Then lay around until she falls asleep.How cuddly are they? 4Favorite toys or games? She like toys that squeaks and balls. Mostly she like to rough house.Tell us a fun story about your foster Charley makes everyone fall in love with her the moment they see her, especially men. I took her to a behavioral trainer and she immediately fell in love with him and he liked her alot. He used her for all his demonstration. She wanted his attention/affection.I love my foster and think he/she is fabulous because _____________? She is so mild mannered. She hardly barks, she only growls when she is playing or someone rings the door bell, she is very loveable, and she is always ready to go. She is the absolute best dog.What makes him/her nervous or unhappy? New people trying to pet her head, someone yelling, or excessively barking dog.Overall, how are your foster's manners? (some examples: Jumps on people? Mouthy? Gets into trash?) She only jumps on people when she is happy to see them and want to play. She is not mouthy because she barley barks, she sniff the trash but does not get into it. She likes to pull on clothes and takes socks off your feet. She will paw you and stare at you to let you know she is bored or to go outside.Does your foster have any behavioral issues or quirks? No major behavioral issues. If you do not take her out when she let's you know she has to relieve herself she will go in the house. She does try to tell you by going to the door multiple times, stand on you, or try to get you out of bed.Does your foster have any medical issues? Yes, a torn muscle in her left hind leg that did not heal properly so it gets stiff. She also has allergies.Anything else you want to share? 9/12/2024 Was easily handled both in the kennel and during the exam. 

11/15/2024 Passing through the kennels this morning and he was jumping and salivating heavily on the door. I walked into the room and he stiffened and hard stared before lunging and snarling at the door, whale eyed, biting at the bars if my hand was nearby while snarling. Later went by to visit him while out in the play yard. He was loose and wiggly at the gate, ignored treats but did allow us to come into the yard. Had zoomies and tried to jump a few times but redirected easily with a "sit" command or back turning. Knows sit, lay down and paw. Brought into the office to dress for DFTD 15 minutes later and he was quickly amped up coming into the office. Pulling, jerking on the leash, heavily stress panting, increasing overarousal. Lynn had to hold the leash firmly and give him several minutes to calm down in order to put the harness and collar on. Incredibly frustrated and pent up with energy. The DFTD was comfortable with taking a hard puller on leash and energetic dog for a trail walk (limited visual on other dogs) so we decided he needed to get out of the kennel for a bit. He did not mouth or bite at any point in the interactions, just very jumpy with high energy spins. Use treats to retrieve from kennel and monitor barrier reactivity. BR observed and level of OA in office is notably concerning. Currently leveled as a L2-OA/JM. Including BR in level.

The foster parent dropped their leash as I held mine with Ricki and with the foster parent's permission I dropped mine. 3/4/2025 Google doc:https://docs.google.com/document/d/12VRZbec5PdplO1XKaDgVG3t8xgSpf__i1z994XBE-vg/edit?usp=sharingPrimary Presenting Issues:Separation AnxietyReactivity to other dogsReactivity to strange menBackground/History:Two year old, 56 lbs, spayed maleTrazodone 100mg 2 tablets, once ever 12 hrs. Theo has been with Nelly for two monthsAverage of 4-5 hrs home alone (without human companionship)Knows sit, lay down, stay, waitTheo seems to do better with strange males in his own house compared to other environments. Nelly described some interactions with other dogs but it’s hard for me to tell if Theo was being playful or aggressive without video of it. For the moment I have asked Nelly to stop dog-to-dog interactions until Theo has some more skills and feels more confident. I am referring Nelly to Malena DeMartini website for separation anxiety help with a licenced professional. Primary Care Veterinarian: LifeLine Animal Shelter Veterinarian Food/Feeding Schedule: Daily Fresh 3 cups a day, 7am, 1pm, 7pm.Medical Issues:No known medical issuesExercise:Out for potty 5 times a day10-15 min walk three times a day30 min walk 1-2 times a dayFetch and walking around the yard 2-3 times a dayTraining:No known formal training historyEquipment:Body harness6 ft leashRecommendations:It is incredibly important to manage Theo’s environment so that he does not get a chance to rehearse the undesirable behaviors. If you see that he has already spotted an other dog approaching, move the other way to gain some distance from the other dog. It’s important to not prompt Theo to perform a cue that he is not ready to perform or has not practice under those circumstances. Remember, practice makes perfect. Practice all the suggested behaviors in different situations and environments where Theo is successful. Slowly practice outdoors as Theo’s confidence increases and starts to offer unprompted check-ins. Practice scenarios that you have experienced in the past without the distraction. Work on distance, distraction and duration as three separate levels of difficulty. See below a list of activities you can do to help Theo with his reactivity and also to meet strangers.Confidence:Sniffing GamesFind it! This is a great game to play encouraging your dog to find a treat (or toy if he has a favorite toy). Show your dog a treat or his favorite toy, and then place it out of his sight but easily accessible. Tell him to “Find it!”. Once he finds it praise enthusiastically. You can start to increase the difficulty of the game by turning off the lights, adding more treats, using boxes or even hiding treats in less conventional places like inside of a shoe. The rewards for the dog are multiple- he gets a treat or finds his toy plus a very happy handler. If issuing a toy, be sure to reward his find with some play before starting again. When multiple treats or toys are used, this particular game helps to build persistence and trust in the handler. The dog may initially find only 2 out of 3 treats, but he quickly discovers that persistence in searching when you give the “Find it!” cue pays off. He learns to believe you - there really is another one there! FreeworkIntroduction to FreeworkPlace snuffle mats and licky mats around an rea of your hours and load them with treats, yogurt, peanut butter, etc… Let your dog go in and explore the area while enjoying the amazing treats you set out for him. Don’t give him big pieces, this activity is more about the journey of finding the treats. Try using small crumbs so encourage more sniffing. You can also use your dog’s kibble for this. This game allows your dog to freely go in an area and explore. You can also do the same set-up outdoors to encourage him to sniff in situations where he might want to bark otherwise. Scatter FeedScatter Feeding Dogs: A Step-by-Step Guide To Our Favourite Calm Enrichment Activity!Why scatter feeding is beneficial for dogsScatter feeding provides a way for Theo to use his nose and calm down. You can use the same cue as “Find it!”. Do this in your back yard or even Sniffspots! Consent TestPetting Consent Tests movieParticing this form of consent testing will help Theo have some predictability when meeting strangers. Knowing that he wont be petted unless requested can be very empowering for dogs. When Theo meets strangers, please encourage your visitors to not do strong eye contact or talk to Theo at least initially. Let Theo do some freework or scatter feet for some minutes while he is adjusting to the presence of the new visitor. Communication:Teach Unprompted Attention/Auto Check-InAuto Check-In.pdfI am attaching a handout on how to do this but here is a short course on how to teach it with some demo videos: https://suzanneclothier.com/shop/autocheckin/This is very similar to the “Look at me” cue with the difference that it’s coming from the inside out where the dog is voluntarily offering attention. Puppy Politeness PokerPractice Puppy Politeness Poker by creating a list of reliable cues Theo will enthusiastically perform. Also create a list of real-life rewards that he will work for (meal time, access to a snuffle mat, opening a door, etc). Utilize those cues to give him explicit permission to access something he wants and change it up every time. This will teach Theo to slow down, listen to your request and work for what he wants. Teaches impulse control, attention and it polishes the communication between you and him. You can learn more about this concept by watching this free webinar: https://suzanneclothier.com/member_video_library/puppy-politeness-poker-webinar/Training:Teaching TouchTouch.pdfOnce Theo is able to give a “Touch” when cued in different situations, you can start using this cue during walks when you see that he spots an other dog and want to prevent him from reacting. You might need to use smellier rewards in the beginning. Practice WaitI don’t have a hand-out for wait but it sounds like Theo already knows this behavior and he just need to practice. Start small with baby steps. Take one step at a time to build distance. Once you are able to ask Theo to wait and go to a different room you can start working on duration. Once Theo is able to wait for a longer period of time you can throw in distractions like maybe closing a door and then opening it. The more you practice this, the easier it will be for him once you take it outside and introduce it in the stairs. Remember to start out with baby steps, even through Theo already has mastered “Wait” with distance, duration and distractions in-doors, you still want to start with just one step outdoors. Management:Teach 1-2-3 Treat! https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ui6dWBDdDScI wasn’t able to find any great videos of this (I should make my own lol) but basically you condition your dog to expect a treat when they hear the word “three”. If you practice this in-doors with no distractions, you eventually will be abe to do this outdoors. When you see another dog coming then you can perform the pattern that Theo already knows and he will prefer to be next to you waiting for the treat instead of reacting to the other dog. Emergency “U” turnTeaching an Emergency U Turn Portland Dog Training/ Teach an Emergency U-Turn for your Reactive Dog/ Noble Woof Dog TrainingTeaching Theo an Emergency “U” turn will help you get out of situations where he is likely to react. By practicing this, you will be able to prevent him from practicing the undesirable behavior. Scatter FeedAfter Theo has had a lot of practice with the “Find it” cue, you can do a scatter feed during walks when you see there is a dog approaching on the opposite site of the street. Please be mindful that this would be done if you are sure that the other dog is not walking towards you or wont approach you. This is meant as a management technique to prevent him from reacting to an other dog and rehearse the undesirable behavior. TouchOnce Theo learns touch, you can also do this to basically step aside and call him over buy asking him to touch. This will allow you to position him an a way where he is not facing the other dog approaching and will buy you some time while the other dog finishes crossing. Follow up:I recommend booking an in-person appointment to work on counter conditioning and desensitizing Theo to other dogs during walks and address reactivity issues. Additionally we can work practicing polite greetings with strangers. To book your next in-person appointment please visit https://loyalpawrenting.pet/ → Book Now → First Let’s Meet → Step 2: In-Home Assessment.During this 1.5 hr visit, we will work on creating a customized training, enrichment and management plan to set up Theo for success. We will also perform a Relationship Assessment Test to determine behavior patterns in your relationship with Theo. If you are interested in self-paced training I recommend taking the following course by Victoria Stillwell: https://positively.com/learning/course/help-stop-reactivity

If you practice this in-doors with no distractions, you eventually will be abe to do this outdoors. When you see another dog coming then you can perform the pattern that Theo already knows and he will prefer to be next to you waiting for the treat instead of reacting to the other dog. Emergency “U” turnTeaching an Emergency U Turn Portland Dog Training/ Teach an Emergency U-Turn for your Reactive Dog/ Noble Woof Dog TrainingTeaching Theo an Emergency “U” turn will help you get out of situations where he is likely to react. By practicing this, you will be able to prevent him from practicing the undesirable behavior. Scatter FeedAfter Theo has had a lot of practice with the “Find it” cue, you can do a scatter feed during walks when you see there is a dog approaching on the opposite site of the street. Please be mindful that this would be done if you are sure that the other dog is not walking towards you or wont approach you. This is meant as a management technique to prevent him from reacting to an other dog and rehearse the undesirable behavior. TouchOnce Theo learns touch, you can also do this to basically step aside and call him over buy asking him to touch. This will allow you to position him an a way where he is not facing the other dog approaching and will buy you some time while the other dog finishes crossing. Follow up:I recommend booking an in-person appointment to work on counter conditioning and desensitizing Theo to other dogs during walks and address reactivity issues. Additionally we can work practicing polite greetings with strangers. We will also perform a Relationship Assessment Test to determine behavior patterns in your relationship with Theo. If you are interested in self-paced training I recommend taking the following course by Victoria Stillwell: https://positively.com/learning/course/help-stop-reactivity

4/9/2025 Kennel staff asked for help getting Cebu into the interior portion of his run for cleaning. As I turned my back he jumped up on me with VERY loose body language with lots of energy eager to  play. Allowed yard time until kennel staff needed to place him back into his run.Once kennel staff was done with run , he was easily leashed from courtyard and walked past kennels with dogs with no reaction. 4/14/2025 Would only approach the door when it was shut at first,when I opened it he would back into the corner and sit. Avoided eye contact and ears stayed back for the most part. Did a lot of sniffing in the yard but would stop and solicit pets periodically. A little hesitant to go back into the kennel but followed me in after some coaxing.

4/19/2025 Cebu does not like the environment may benefit in being in a more calm room (79) once leveled down . He rather sit on the exterior portion of his kennel or in the very back corner. Food/ meds may need to be placed in the back of the kennel. Does not like to be re-kenneled on the inside and will hesitate but will allow you to re-kennel with out incident.

She said he was initially a little difficult to leash, but once he got outside he was soliciting attention from me (only met him twice before) and actually jumped up on a volunteer he had never met that approached. Enjoyed being pet and kept sitting in front of me like he wanted more pets. Suggest leveling down to L2 and moving from 200s.
